text: Section 3(a) excludes: 'An invention the primary or intended use or commercial exploitation of which could be contrary to public order or morality or which causes serious prejudice to human, animal or plant life or health or to the environment.' Examples: inventions for illegal activities, weapons of mass destruction, torture devices. For AYUSH: unlikely to apply unless product is inherently harmful or intended for illegal use. Safety data supporting no adverse effects strengthens position against any 3(a) challenge.

Section 3(b) excludes: 'A discovery, scientific theory or mathematical method.' Discovery: finding something existing in nature. Invention: creating something new. Example: discovering a new compound in a plant = discovery (not patentable). Isolating that compound through novel process = may be invention. For AYUSH: merely discovering that neem has antibacterial property is not patentable; creating a specific formulation using that property may be patentable.

section: Section 3(c) Mere Discovery of Living Things
text: Section 3(c) excludes: 'Mere discovery of a scientific principle or the formulation of an abstract theory or discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature.' Covers: scientific principles, abstract theories, natural substances. For AYUSH: finding a new medicinal plant species is discovery (not patentable). Extracting and formulating its active compounds may be invention. Patent the process and formulation, not the plant itself.

Section 3(d) excludes: 'Mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance or mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.' Critical for AYUSH: new forms (salts, polymorphs, isomers) of known herbs/compounds need enhanced THERAPEUTIC efficacy data per Novartis ruling. Better bioavailability alone insufficient without clinical efficacy improvement.

After Novartis v. India (2013), Section 3(d) efficacy means THERAPEUTIC efficacy for pharmaceuticals. To overcome: 1) Provide comparative clinical/preclinical data. 2) Show the new form is therapeutically better (lower dose, faster action, fewer side effects, better patient outcomes). 3) Physical property improvements (solubility, stability) help only if translated to therapeutic benefit. For AYUSH formulations: if claiming enhanced bioavailability of turmeric nanoparticles, show this leads to better therapeutic outcome in target condition.

Section 3(e) excludes: 'A substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof or a process for producing such substance.' Key phrase: 'aggregation of properties' vs synergy. If combining herbs A and B just gives you A's properties + B's properties, it's mere admixture. If combination produces unexpected enhanced effect beyond sum, it's potentially patentable. For AYUSH polyherbal: synergy data (isobolograms, combination index) essential.

Section 3(h) excludes: 'A method of agriculture or horticulture.' Covers: cultivation methods, planting techniques, harvesting methods. Does NOT exclude: agricultural machinery, compositions (fertilizers, pesticides), storage methods. For AYUSH medicinal plant cultivation: the method of growing ashwagandha is not patentable, but novel fertilizer compositions, processing methods, or equipment may be.

Section 3(i) excludes: 'Any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings or any process for a similar treatment of animals to render them free of disease or to increase their economic value or that of their products.' Methods of treatment are NOT patentable in India. For AYUSH: cannot patent 'a method of treating diabetes by administering Ashwagandha'. Can patent: the formulation itself, Swiss-type claims ('use of X for manufacture of medicament for Y').

Section 3(j) excludes: 'Plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms but including seeds, varieties and species and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals.' Plants/animals/seeds not patentable. Micro-organisms may be patentable. For AYUSH: cannot patent medicinal plants themselves. Can patent: extraction processes, formulations using plant extracts, micro-organism derived products (fermentation).

Section 3(k) excludes: 'A mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms.' Software 'per se' excluded; software with technical application may qualify. For AYUSH: AI/ML algorithms for formulation optimization are likely not patentable per se. Hardware + software combinations, medical devices with embedded software may be patentable. Consider trade secret protection for proprietary algorithms.

Section 3(p) excludes: 'An invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components.' Direct codification of TK as prior art. Covers both: exact traditional formulations AND aggregations duplicating known traditional properties. For AYUSH: most challenged provision. Defense: show novel aspect (processing, ratio, delivery) not in traditional knowledge, provide TKDL search showing no anticipation.

Strategy for overcoming Section 3 objections: 1) Section 3(d) — provide comparative therapeutic efficacy data. 2) Section 3(e) — demonstrate synergy with isobolograms, combination index. 3) Section 3(p) — distinguish from prior TK with novel processing, ratios, evidence. 4) General — narrow claims to patentable aspects, amend to exclude non-patentable subject matter, provide detailed technical arguments. Always address each objection specifically with data and legal reasoning.

Draft claims to avoid Section 3 issues: 1) Focus on novel aspects — specific process conditions, novel delivery systems, unexpected results. 2) Avoid claiming known substances per se — claim the formulation/composition. 3) Include specific parameters — ratios, particle sizes, processing conditions. 4) Swiss-type claims for use inventions ('use of X for manufacture of medicament for Y'). 5) Product-by-process claims when process is novel. 6) Include data in specification supporting novelty over traditional knowledge and enhanced efficacy.

How examiners cite Section 3: FER will identify specific Section 3 ground and typically cite references. For 3(d): prior patent/publication showing known substance, argue new form. For 3(p): TKDL citation or classical text reference. For 3(e): argue components known, combination obvious. Response strategy: address the specific citation, distinguish technically, provide data where required. Generic denials don't work; engage substantively with each objection.

Section 3 grounds in patent opposition: Opponents frequently cite Section 3 to invalidate AYUSH patents. Most common: 3(p) — traditional knowledge from TKDL/classical texts, 3(d) — no enhanced efficacy for new forms, 3(e) — mere admixture. Defense: maintain strong prosecution record with data, anticipate challenges during drafting. Attack: search TKDL and classical texts for opponent's patents, challenge weak patents through opposition.
